title: A split Borel pair for a semisimple group over an arbitrary field
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field]. Let $G$ be a smooth connected affine group scheme of finite type over $k$ [def-sc-group-scheme], semisimple in the following sense: over an algebraic closure there is no nontrivial smooth connected solvable normal closed subgroup; solvable means that successive commutator subgroup schemes eventually become trivial. Let $T\subseteq G$ be a split maximal torus, namely a closed subgroup isomorphic over $k$ to $\mathbf G_m^r$ for $r\geq0$, maximal among tori after algebraic closure, where $\mathbf G_m(A)=A^\times$. There exist smooth geometrically connected closed $k$-subgroups $T\subseteq B\subseteq G$ and $U\subseteq B$, and a $k$-group homomorphism $p:B\to T$, with the following properties. The group $B$ is split solvable as in [def-sfb-split-solvable-right-torsors]: it has a finite descending series of smooth connected closed subgroups normal in their predecessor, with represented fppf quotients $\mathbf G_a$ or $\mathbf G_m$. For every algebraically closed extension $F/k$, the subgroup $B_F$ is maximal among smooth connected solvable closed subgroups of $G_F$, and $U_F$ is its largest smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup. The group $U$ is unipotent: its geometric points are unipotent matrices in a faithful finite-dimensional matrix representation, meaning $(u-I)^N=0$ for some $N\geq1$. The map $p$ restricts to the identity on $T$, has scheme-theoretic kernel $U$, and multiplication induces an isomorphism $U\rtimes T\xrightarrow{\sim}B$, $(u,t)\mapsto ut$, with multiplication $(u,t)(u',t')=(utu't^{-1},tt')$. All these subgroup inclusions, the projection, and this decomposition remain such after every field extension of $k$. Neither characteristic zero nor perfection nor simple connectedness is assumed.

source.place: Corollaries 21.30 and 21.34, printed pp.434--435; Theorem 21.32 and Corollary 21.33, pp.434--435 (geometric Borel condition); Theorem 13.33(a),(b),(e), printed pp.265--266, and the proof of 21.34 (unipotent radical and torus decomposition). Semisimple special case of the split reductive assertions.

proof.text: First establish the geometric reductivity needed below. The identity of $G$ is a $k$-point, so [lem-sbc-connected-rational-point-geometrically-connected] makes $G$ geometrically connected. Over an algebraic closure $\bar k$, the stated semisimplicity hypothesis and the last assertion of [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure] imply that $G_{\bar k}$ is reductive. Thus $G$ is reductive over $k$: it is smooth affine geometrically connected of finite type, and $G_{\bar k}$ has no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup. Moreover [lem-sfb-geometric-neutral-reductivity-field-invariance], applied to $G$ and any algebraically closed extension $F/k$, makes $G_F$ reductive: its identity component is all of $G_F$ by geometric connectedness. All groups here are smooth affine of finite type, as required by that invariance statement.

source.place: Definition 19.22 and the following paragraph, p.402; Proposition 1.34, pp.16-17 (geometric connectedness); geometric-reductivity input as stated in the cited node.

proof.text: Choose an isomorphism $T\simeq\mathbf G_m^r$. By [lem-sfb-affine-group-dual-number-calculus] the conjugation action of $G$ on $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(G)$, a finite-dimensional tangent space, is a homomorphism of group schemes $\operatorname{Ad}_G:G\to\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak g)$; restrict it to $T$. Apply [lem-sfb-split-torus-representation-weight-decomposition] to this representation; let $\Phi$ be its finite set of nonzero characters. By [lem-sfb-relative-split-torus-matrix-sheaf], each $\alpha\in\Phi$ is an integer row $(a_0,\ldots,a_{r-1})$, and integer columns give cocharacters. Choose a positive integer $N$ larger than $1+\sum_i|a_i|$ for every row in $\Phi$ and take $\lambda(t)=(t,t^N,\ldots,t^{N^{r-1}})$. If $a_j$ is the last nonzero coefficient, then $|a_j|N^j\geq N^j>\sum_{i<j}|a_i|N^i$, so $\langle\alpha,\lambda\rangle\ne0$. If $\Phi$ is empty take $\lambda=0$, including $r=0$. These are integer pairings, not their reductions in $k$. This regularity persists over every extension $L/k$. For an $L$-algebra $R$ one has $G_L(R)=G(R)$, so the bijections $E_{G,R}$ and $E_{G_L,R}$ of [lem-sfb-affine-group-dual-number-calculus] have the same target; the composite $E_{G_L,R}^{-1}E_{G,R}:\mathfrak g\otimes_kR\to\operatorname{Lie}(G_L)\otimes_LR$ is additive, $R$-linear by the scaling clause, natural in $R$, and by the characterizing identity of $\operatorname{Ad}$ it intertwines $\operatorname{Ad}_G(t)$ and $\operatorname{Ad}_{G_L}(t)$ for $t\in T(R)$. (Over $R=L$ this is the identification $L\otimes_k\mathfrak g\cong\operatorname{Lie}(G_L)$ of [lem-sfb-affine-group-lie-tangent-calculus].) Hence the tensored weight basis diagonalizes $\operatorname{Ad}_{G_L}|_{T_L}$ with the same monomials on the diagonal, so the nonzero weights of $T_L$ in $\operatorname{Lie}(G_L)$ are exactly $\Phi$, with the same integer labels.

source.place: Corollary 21.30, p.434 (choice of regular cocharacter); Theorem 12.12, pp.234-235 (weight basis); Theorem 12.9, pp.233-234 (integer characters); Section 10.19, p.192 (tangent scalar extension).

proof.text: Use [lem-sfb-reductive-cocharacter-parabolic-geometry] for $G$ and this $\lambda$. Its limit functors give smooth geometrically connected closed subgroups $B:=P_\lambda$ and $U:=U_\lambda$, with $U$ normal in $B$, and the evaluation homomorphism $r_\lambda:P_\lambda\to Z_\lambda$. The torus $T$ is maximal in $G$ over $k$, since it is maximal after extension to $\bar k$ ([lem-sfb-maximal-torus-field-extension]). Since $T$ is split maximal and $\lambda$ has nonzero pairing with every nontrivial adjoint weight, the last clause of that node gives $Z_\lambda=T$. Set $p=r_\lambda$ with this target. The same node says that $p|_T=\mathrm{id}$, that its scheme-theoretic kernel is $U$, that $U$ is split unipotent, and that multiplication $U\rtimes T\to B$ is an isomorphism with product $(u,t)(u',t')=(utu't^{-1},tt')$. In particular these are statements on subgroup schemes and on all test algebras, not just on geometric points.

source.place: Theorem 13.33(a),(b),(e), pp.265-266; Proposition 17.60, p.372; proof of Proposition 21.29, pp.433-434; proof of Corollary 21.34, p.435.

proof.text: Let $F/k$ be any algebraically closed extension. Step 1 gives the reductivity of $G_F$. By [lem-sfb-maximal-torus-field-extension], $T_F$ is maximal: maximality over $\bar k$, which is a hypothesis of the item, first implies maximality over $k$ and then over $F$. It is split by the chosen monomial-coordinate model. The cocharacter $\lambda_F$ is regular by step 2. Therefore [lem-sfb-regular-cocharacter-borel-description] says that $P_{\lambda_F}$ is a maximal smooth connected solvable closed subgroup of $G_F$. Formation of the limit subgroups commutes with every field extension by [lem-sfb-reductive-cocharacter-parabolic-geometry], so $P_{\lambda_F}=B_F$. This proves precisely the required geometric Borel condition. The same base-change assertion gives $U_L=U_{\lambda_L}$, $(Z_\lambda)_L=T_L$, and $p_L=r_{\lambda_L}$ for every field extension $L/k$; the semidirect-product isomorphism and all its subgroup maps extend to the identical formulas over $L$.

source.place: Proposition 21.29 and Corollary 21.30, pp.433-434; Theorem 21.32 and Corollary 21.33, pp.434-435; Theorem 17.82, p.379; the defining limit functors of Section 13d.

proof.text: Construct the actual split-solvable series, rather than infer it merely from solvability. In $T=\mathbf G_m^r$ let $T_j$ be the subgroup with the first $j$ coordinates $1$, for $0\leq j\leq r$. Start with $B_j=p^{-1}(T_j)$; thus $B_0=B$ and $B_r=U$. The coordinate projection $p$ identifies the fppf quotient $B/U$ with $T$: $p$ has a section and two points over the same base point differ by exactly one element of $U$. Apply [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry] to $U\triangleleft B$ and the subgroups $T_j$. It gives closed smooth connected inverse images $B_j=U\rtimes T_j$. Here $T_j\simeq\mathbf G_m^{r-j}$ is smooth and connected: its Laurent-coordinate chart is a localization of a polynomial algebra, and its coordinate algebra is a domain. Each $B_{j+1}$ is normal in $B_j$: it is the kernel of the homomorphism given by coordinate $j+1$ of $p$. This coordinate map presents the fppf quotient $B_j/B_{j+1}=\mathbf G_m$: on underlying schemes it is the product projection $U\times T_{j+1}\times\mathbf G_m\to\mathbf G_m$, and two lifts with the same coordinate differ by exactly one element of its kernel. Append the split-unipotent series of $U$ from step 3, whose successive represented fppf quotients are $\mathbf G_a$. This concatenated finite series has precisely the properties in [def-sfb-split-solvable-right-torsors]. Over any field extension the same coordinate projections and kernel identities still present these quotients. The factors of the appended series remain connected by [lem-sbc-connected-rational-point-geometrically-connected], applied to their identity sections. Smoothness is preserved by base change ([lem-pc-proper-base-change], clause (2)). Zero-length series cause no problem when $r=0$ or $U=1$.

source.place: Proof of Corollary 21.34, p.435; split-series definition 6.33, pp.132-133; elementary coordinate construction; connected base change: Stacks Tag 04KV; smooth base change: Stacks Tag 01VB. Quotient correspondence: Theorem 5.55, p.113, and Proposition 5.59, p.114.

proof.text: Finally, fix any algebraically closed extension $F/k$. First, $U$ is unipotent in the sense of a closed group immersion into the upper unitriangular group $\mathcal U_{n,k}$: by induction along the split series $U=U_0\supseteq\cdots\supseteq U_m=1$ of step 3, starting from $U_m=1\subseteq\mathcal U_{1,k}$ and using that $\mathbf G_a\to\mathcal U_{2,k}$, $a\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}1&a\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, is a closed group immersion, [lem-sfb-unipotent-extension-arbitrary] applied to $U_{i+1}\triangleleft U_i\to\mathbf G_a$ makes each $U_i$ unipotent. Base change of such an immersion is again one, so $U$ is unipotent in the sense of [lem-sfb-unipotent-to-multiplicative-trivial]. The group $U_F$ is smooth connected normal in $B_F$ and unipotent, by step 3 and its field-extension compatibility in step 4. If $V\subseteq B_F$ is any smooth connected normal unipotent closed subgroup, then [lem-sfb-unipotent-to-multiplicative-trivial] applies to $p_F|_V:V\to T_F$, because $T_F$ is a split torus and hence of multiplicative type. This homomorphism is trivial on every test algebra; consequently $V\subseteq\ker(p_F)=U_F$ scheme-theoretically. Thus $U_F$ is the largest such subgroup. The unipotence convention in the cited node is equivalent, for smooth groups, to the faithful-matrix geometric-point condition required in the item. It also asserts that unipotence is preserved by every field extension. Together with steps 3-5 this verifies every requested clause, over $k$ and after every field extension, without any characteristic, perfection or simple-connectedness restriction.
